rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of a prince
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince should manage the public, not his private interest; study nothing but the common good; obey the laws he authors; take account of the administration of magistrates and subordinate officers; set a watch over himself against pleasure, liberty, flattery, and excess; remember he will be called to account for every trespass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage guidance: 'He that takes a scepter in his hand should manage the public, not his private, interest; study nothing but the common good; and not in the least go contrary to those laws whereof himself is both the author and exactor... he should the more diligently endeavor and set a watch over himself, lest perhaps he be led aside and fail in his duty.' Anti-patterns: hunting daily, selling dignities, draining citizens' purses, seeking private profit under names of equity; measuring everything by personal will and profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical and pastoral duties over ceremonies
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian ministers should practise faith and charity, instruct and care for their flock, and not substitute cowls, odd prayers, fastings, ceremonies, or titles for the real duties of ministry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations/examples: 'I promised... not to cowls, odd prayers, and fastings, but to the duties of faith and charity.' Anti-patterns described include perfunctory prayers, leaving care of flock to suffragans or vicars, prioritizing ceremonies and titles over teaching and charity, and treating ecclesiastical office as an occasion for profit and ease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of clerical vestments and symbols should correspond to conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Vestments and emblems (alb, miter, gloves, crosier, cross, purple robe) have moral-symbolic meanings (blameless life, knowledge of Scripture, sincere administration of sacraments, care for the flock, victory over earthly affections, charity) and should reflect actual virtuous conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the text: 'what their Albe should put them in mind of, to wit a blameless life; what is meant by their forked miters... a perfect knowledge of the Old and New Testaments; what those gloves on their hands, but a sincere administration of the Sacraments; what their crosier, but a careful looking after the flock... what the cross born before them, but victory over all earthly affections.' Anti-pattern: wearing these symbols while living in luxury, neglecting pastoral care, and accumulating wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good preaching: insist on Scripture and maintain coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Preachers should focus firmly on Scripture and coherent narration rather than using irrelevant preambles, grammatical curiosities, or tangential questions; the Scriptural text should be the main matter insisted upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text critique: 'they bring in instead of narration some texts of Scripture, but handle them cursorily, and as it were by the bye, when yet it is the only thing they should have insisted on.' Anti-patterns enumerated: invoking poets irrelevantly; long grammatical or etymological digressions (e.g., splitting the name Jesus into mystical letters); inserting irrelevant theological questions; handling texts cursorily; concluding with allegorical fables unrelated to the core scriptural message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratorical delivery: avoid noisy affectation and mismatched performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Orators should not favour noisy, excessive, or affectatious delivery (loudness, extreme voice shifts, caricatured gestures, pointless jests) that drowns understanding or flatters the audience rather than conveying truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the passage: 'they begin theirs at that rate they can scarce hear themselves... to move the affections a louder voice is requisite... use a strange contention of voice... prick in a jest here and there; but... so void of wit and so little to the purpose.' Examples of bad performance: singing out words, skipping up and down, making new faces, inserting weak jests or flattery disguised as freedom of speech. Good delivery should be sober, grave, and matched to content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rhetorical pedantry and empty scholasticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not substitute technical learning, pompous titles, or abstruse syllogisms for substantive argument or pastoral care; rhetoric that is 'wide of the matter' and pedantic impresses but fails to instruct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer condemns introductions 'wide of the matter', the parade of titles ('most subtle doctors', 'seraphic doctors'), and the tossing about of 'syllogisms, majors, minors, conclusions... so weak and foolish that they are below pedantry.' Guidance: prefer clarity, relevance, and meaningful exposition over display of scholastic tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church governance should not rely on worldly power and wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church should not govern by sword, pursuit of riches, or worldly honors; its business should be spiritual instruction, poverty, tears, prayers, and service rather than accumulation of lands, tributes, and armed defense of patrimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique in text: 'they govern all by the sword... they contend with fire and sword... gather the harvest of money... with the very sight of which they sink men's souls.' Anti-patterns: using excommunications, interdictions, executions in effigy, and war to defend temporal patrimony; placing administration of spiritual duties under layers of officials while enriching the See.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical method: inversion, authoritative citation, and ironic praise
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful satire can praise what is usually condemned (folly) by deploying inversion and irony, supported by classical and biblical authorities, thereby exposing hypocrisy and societal absurdities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The oration uses classical (Horace, Cicero, Homer) and biblical (Ecclesiastes, Jeremiah, Solomon, Paul) quotations and proverbs to argue paradoxically that folly is pervasive and often rewarded: e.g., 'The number of fools is infinite.' Technique guidance: marshal authoritative quotations, proverbs, and scriptural citations and use them ironically to bolster the satirical claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid exemplification, listing, and hyperbole to ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridicule and satire are sharpened by concrete, grotesque examples, long lists of absurdities, and hyperbolic imagery that make the vices described appear ridiculous and thereby instructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in text: 'a large trough full of all kinds of fish; another tumble you out so many bushels of prayers; another... bundles of ceremonies; another wears a cowl so lined with grease...' Guidance: accumulate sensory, comic, or shocking particulars and contrast them with the supposed ideals (symbols, titles) to heighten irony.
